newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss-Belgian balloon takes off to circle globe.
newsitem.headline: Swiss-Belgian balloon takes off to circle globe.

text.p: A Swiss psychiatrist and a Belgian photographer-pilot took off from a snow-covered Alpine meadow on Sunday in a bid to become the first men to circle the world in a balloon.

As the silver-grey Breitling Orbiter lifted skywards at 8.55 a.m. (0755 GMT), its crew Bertrand Piccard and Wim Verstraeten were cheered by hundreds of onlookers including British tycoon Richard Branson, who failed in a similar bid last week.

"Pray for us, we'll need it," Piccard told the crowd from the top of the yellow, pressurised cabin under the helium-filled balloon just minutes earlier as the sun rose over surrounding mountain peaks.
Village churches rang their bells as the balloon lifted off.

"I wish I were going with them, but my wife won't let me," said a smiling Branson, whose own balloon crash-landed in Algeria last week only a day after it took off from Morocco. "But I wish them all the luck."

The 38-year-old Piccard, whose father and grandfather won world fame as explorers of the stratosphere and the ocean depths, and Verstraeten, 39, have already taken a balloon across the Atlantic together, in 1992.

The Orbiter, constructed in Britain, rose swiftly when restraining ropes were removed and was seen heading westwards towards Lake Geneva. It was then due to head south-east over France and Italy towards the eastern Mediterranean.

At a height of around 10,000 metres (30,000 feet), Piccard and Verstraeten must ensure they join jet-stream air currents between the 30th and 40th northern parallels to complete the flight in the target time of 14 days.

If all goes well, the route will take them over Turkey and Iran, Afghanistan, China and Japan. Then they head out over the Pacific to the United States and back across the Atlantic to Europe, or possibly North Africa.

In emotional scenes before takeoff, briefly delayed when the gas burners over the capsule failed to ignite, Piccard hugged his tearful wife Michele and their three small daughters and Verstraeten embraced his wife Dominique and their son.
"I must admit I'm very nervous, but once we're up there there will be so much to do I won't be thinking about it," said the dark-haired, balding Piccard.

The burners, which will keep hot air pumping up into the balloon at night, were lit by a flame from a torch brought from the Olympic Museum in Lausanne, Piccard's home city and headquarters of the International Olympic Committee (IOC).
The IOC, whose own five-ring symbol is etched on the Orbiter's outer aluminium cover, has asked Piccard to use the flight to symbolise sport as a messenger of peace.
During the day, the pair will rely on the lift of the balloon and solar power gathered by panels strung along the side of their capsule to keep them aloft.
Branson, whose own round-the-world bid from Morocco in a much larger craft lasted less than 24 hours, swapped experiences with the two balloonists just before the lift-off.

"I came to wish them well. We tried and failed, but they have a lovely balloon and I hope they succeed," he told a Swiss television interviewer on the field at Chateau d'Oex, a ski resort which hosts an annual balloon festival.
"We went for a very high-tech approach and it didn't work. But we'll definitely try again if Breitling doesn't make it."

Piccard's father Jacques, a professor who holds the world deep-sea diving record aboard a bathyscape built by his own father Auguste, said there was "always a lot of luck" in new missions of this type.

Watching the take-off preparations with his grandchildren, he recalled being taken at the age of 10 to see his father take off in 1932 in a balloon from a field near Zurich and become the first man to reach the stratosphere.
